title: Loops + Decisions
summary: Combine `for` loops with `if`/`else` — so each step of the loop can make its own choice.

content.title: Checking Inside Every Step
content.summary: An `if` statement inside a loop runs a check on every single iteration.
content.body: You can put an `if` statement inside a loop. Python checks the condition every time the loop runs:
content.note:
**Output:**
```
Empty room...
Empty room...
Treasure!
Empty room...
Empty room...
```

The loop runs 5 times. On step `2` it finds treasure; all other steps find nothing.

content.title: Even and Odd
content.summary: The `%` operator gives the remainder after dividing — useful for detecting every other step.
content.body:
A useful trick: the `%` operator gives you the **remainder after dividing**.

For example, 7 ÷ 2 is 3 with `1` left over — so `7 % 2` is `1`. And 4 ÷ 2 is exactly 2 with nothing left over — so `4 % 2` is `0`.

That means `i % 2 == 0` is true for **even** numbers and false for **odd** ones:
content.note: This checks every number from `0` to `5`.

content.title: The Danger Zone
content.summary: Mark a specific loop step as special using `if i == number`.
content.body: You can mark specific loop steps as special:
content.note:
**Output:**
```
Room 1 — safe.
Room 2 — safe.
Warning! Danger zone!
Room 4 — safe.
Room 5 — safe.
```

Each room gets checked. Only room `3` triggers the warning.

content.title: More Than Two Choices: `elif`
content.summary: Use `elif` to handle a third (or fourth, or fifth...) path.
content.body: `if`/`else` gives you two paths. What if you need three? Python has another word: `elif` (short for "else if"). Python checks each one in order, and runs the first one that's true:
content.note: You can have as many `elif` lines as you want between `if` and `else`. Order matters — Python uses the first one that matches.

content.title: Errors You Might See
content.summary: Three common errors, three quick fixes.
content.body:
Loops with decisions inside are a common place for mistakes. Watch for:

• `SyntaxError` — check for a missing `:` after `for`, `if`, `elif`, or `else`.
• `IndentationError` — code inside the loop is 4 spaces in; code inside an `if` inside the loop is **8** spaces in.
• `TypeError` from `+` — you can't do `"Room " + i` because `i` is a number. Use commas inside `print()` instead.

Errors aren't failures — they're Python pointing at the line to look at.

content.title: Indentation Stacks Up
content.summary: Loop body is 4 spaces in. Code inside `if`/`else` inside the loop is 8 spaces in.
content.body: When you nest `if` inside a loop, both need proper indentation:
content.note: The loop body is at 4 spaces. The `if`/`else` bodies are at 8 spaces.

steps.instruction: Step 1: Loop through 6 rooms numbered 1 through 6. Use `range(1, 7)`. Inside the loop, print something like `"Room", i, "— clear."` for every room.
steps.starterCode:
# Walk through 6 dungeon rooms
# Room 4 has the boss!

steps.instruction: Step 2: Add an `if`/`else` **inside** the loop so that when the room is `4`, you print `"Boss fight!"` instead. All other rooms keep their normal message. Remember: the `if` body needs to be indented 8 spaces (4 for the loop, 4 more for the `if`).

bonusSteps.instruction: Bonus: Add a second special room. If the room is `2`, print `"Hidden chest!"`. Use `elif` (from the lesson) so the `if`, the `elif`, and the `else` all chain together.

progressiveHints: Step 1: Use `for i in range(1, 7):` so rooms are numbered 1 through 6.
Step 2: Add `if i == 4:` inside the loop, with `print("Boss fight!")` indented twice. Then put the existing print in an `else:`.
